Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Open Hands is the universal gesture of giving and receiving. The brand sits on the human action at the center of every nonprofit's work. Modern, warm, and immediately legible without religious or political coding.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern nonprofits are competing for attention and donor relationships in a category that has been polished by professionalized fundraising. Donors are design-literate, slightly cynical about overhead, and reward organizations that show clear program work and direct outcomes.
Modern.competitorLandscape: GiveDirectly (givedirectly.org) holds the modern direct-cash-transfer peer position. Charity: Water (charitywater.org) sits in the design-led-fundraising tier. The Trevor Project (thetrevorproject.org) does the cultural-mission middle. We sit closest to GiveDirectly in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A nonprofit that shows the program before the appeal.
Modern.positioningRationale: Most nonprofits lead with the donor's feeling. We lead with the program work. The brand promise is that the donor can see exactly what their gift funds before they give.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Already gives to two or three nonprofits annually. Reads charity-evaluator sites. Values transparency on overhead and program outcomes. Will become a recurring donor if the program work is visible.

dos: Speak to the donor as an adult

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is two thin parallel arcs suggesting open palms, used as the favicon, the donation receipt seal, and the program-report cover.

colorPalette.name: Open Black
colorPalette.meaning: Ink, the work on the page.

typography.primary: Inter for the website and donation flow
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed annual reports
typography.rationale: Inter handles the donation flow and digital surfaces. The serif handles the printed annual report and program documentation.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No guilt-based fundraising. No beneficiary photography that strips dignity. No overhead-shaming campaigns aimed at peers. No celebrity ambassadors.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A site that shows program work first. A printed annual report with the program data and the financials side by side. A quarterly email update written like a project status, not a fundraising appeal.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Three words. The Whitcombe Trust reads as a small, established private foundation. Definite article + family-feeling surname + Trust. The whole name sounds like an institution that has been giving carefully for several generations.
Luxury.story: The Whitcombe Trust was founded by a single family wanting to direct their giving more carefully than mass-market vehicles allowed. The trust accepts no public donations. The endowment is small relative to the giants. The program work is precise.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end philanthropy has been moving toward larger foundations and bigger announcements. There's a parallel market for small family trusts in the older tradition. Smaller endowments, careful grant-making, long-term relationships with grantees. The donor is paying for the trustees, not the brand.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Pew Charitable Trusts (pewtrusts.org) holds the institutional foundation peer. Rockefeller Brothers Fund (rbf.org) sits at the family-foundation tier. Wellcome Trust (wellcome.org) is the international peer. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small private trust making considered grants to a limited number of grantees.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy family principals, trustees, and foundation officers managing significant family philanthropy. They value the trustees' judgment and the long relationship with grantees over the announcement of giving.

dos: Address grantees and trustees by surname
Speak in the language of the discipline
Send paper letters and printed reports
donts: Photograph grantees for press without consent

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn family-crest hallmark, two horizontal lines suggesting a heraldic chief, used on letterhead, the grant documents, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

colorPalette.name: Trust Green
colorPalette.meaning: Old leather, library walls, the trustees' room.

colorPalette.name: Heritage Brass
colorPalette.meaning: Aged metal. The plaque outside the office.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and printed material
typography.secondary: Söhne for the secure grant management portal
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the few digital surfaces.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No public fundraising. No celebrity trustees. No social media presence. No press strategy. No publicly listed grantees without their explicit consent.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word, single verb. Give is what the customer is doing. The brand sits on the action, not the cause, not the institution. Plain, direct, and almost confrontationally simple in a category that usually over-decorates.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most nonprofit brands have elaborate names, mission statements, and donor stories. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the verb itself.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most nonprofit brands fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some giving-circle traditions and the no-name aesthetic of certain donor-advised-fund operators.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A nonprofit with one program, one financial line, and one verb.

targetAudience.primary: Donors who already give and don't want a relationship with the nonprofit. They want to give, see the receipt, and move on.

dos: Show the program, the cost, the impact
Confirm the gift in one line

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. GIVE in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, four letters with generous space. No icon. The donation page, the receipt, and the annual report all carry the wordmark and nothing else.

typography.rationale: One face. The donation page, the receipt, and the annual report all carry the same wordmark.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No monthly fundraising appeals. No donor walls. No gala. No newsletter. No social media presence.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Bedrock signals foundation, permanence, and seriousness. Impact Group names the category. The whole name reads like a real, established philanthropy-services firm already on the panel at major foundations, family offices, and corporate social impact teams.
Corporate.industrySummary: Strategic philanthropy and impact services is a B2B category serving foundations, family offices, and corporate social impact teams. Buyers want partners who can deliver strategy, grant-making infrastructure, and outcomes measurement at institutional scale.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Arabella Advisors (arabellaadvisors.com) holds the philanthropy services peer position. Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors (rockpa.org) sits at the institutional tier. Tideline (tideline.com) does the impact-investing-led middle. We sit smaller and more focused on the contemporary mid-size foundation client.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Strategic philanthropy services for mid-size foundations, family offices, and corporate social impact teams.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Mid-size foundations and family offices are too small for the giant philanthropy advisors and too sophisticated for boutique consultants. We sit between them, with operating discipline and strategic depth.

targetAudience.primary: Foundation Presidents, Chief Impact Officers, and Family Office Principals managing philanthropic capital of $50M to $5B. They sign multi-year advisory contracts.
motivations: Operating infrastructure for grant-making at scale

dos: Show case studies with measured impact
Speak to the principal, not the public

messagingPillars.name: Strategy first
messagingPillars.description: We start with the philanthropic strategy, not the grant-making mechanics.

messagingPillars.name: Operating infrastructure
messagingPillars.description: Grant-making operations, due diligence, and outcomes tracking built for institutional scale.

messagingPillars.name: Reporting that satisfies trustees
messagingPillars.description: Quarterly impact reports formatted for the board and the family principals together.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single solid square base with a smaller square above, suggesting layered bedrock. Reads cleanly on a procurement deck, name badge, and quiet trustee meeting.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and B2B materials
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed quarterly reports
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles formal quarterly trustee reports and printed strategy documents.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No public fundraising. No D2C donor product. No celebrity ambassadors. The firm sells through institutional philanthropy procurement, not public-facing campaigns.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Do Good is the plainest version of what every nonprofit asks people to do. The brand puts the imperative in the brand position. Loud, plain, slightly self-aware about the simplicity, and immediately legible to anyone scrolling past.
Creative.manifesto: Most nonprofit brands sound like they wish they were more polished than they are. They moralize. They overuse stock photography. They send guilt by email. We made Do Good because the actual work of helping people is loud, fun, exhausting, and worth telling friends about. The brand is for the people who help and also have fun doing it.
Creative.industrySummary: Nonprofit branding has been earnest, beige, and slightly preachy. There's room for a brand that's loud, warm, sticker-friendly, and still serious about the program work that justifies the existence of any nonprofit.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Charity: Water (charitywater.org) does design-led nonprofit well. Pencils of Promise (pencilsofpromise.org) holds the millennial-fundraising peer. The Bail Project (bailproject.org) does the loud-mission middle. We sit warmer and louder than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A nonprofit brand that treats the program work as fun.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Already gives to one or two nonprofits. Joins things. Wears the merch. Tells friends about the program. Wants the nonprofit to be a part of their social life, not a guilt trip.

dos: Talk to the donor as a friend who'd help

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display serif with the O of GOOD stylized as a small smile curve. Standalone smile-curve icon for stickers, social profiles, and the back of every donation receipt.

colorPalette.name: Good Yellow
colorPalette.usage: Primary brand color, hero surfaces, stickers

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and big display
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and donation receipts
typography.rationale: Migra has warmth and character. Neue Montreal handles the practical bits. The pair feels designed and human.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not a guilt-based fundraising brand. Not a polished glossy nonprofit. Not afraid of yellow. Not too cool to put a sticker on a tote.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Real customer stories in every appeal. Stickers in every donation envelope. A monthly newsletter that's mostly program updates and one funny aside. Real-world events that mix volunteering and just hanging out. A merch line for the people who actually show up.
